title: The Anatomy of a Convergence Delta: Closing the Correlation Gap Between P&R and Sign-Off
gist: SemiWiki guest piece (byline Vignesh Sunderrajan) dissects the 'convergence delta' between P&R and sign-off STA slack, tracing it to three transitions (extraction, placement-to-routing, pre/post-CTS) and arguing for path-level correlation analysis and shifting sign-off modeling early to avoid costly late ECOs.

insights.claim: In chip physical design, the 'convergence delta' is the per-path slack difference (in picoseconds, signed) between what place-and-route (P&R) reports and what sign-off static timing analysis (STA) reports for the same path, design and stage.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Defines the core metric behind late timing-closure surprises that drive tapeout schedule slips and EDA tool value.
insights.quote: It is measured path by path, in picoseconds, and it has a sign.
insights.locator: A convergence delta is the difference

insights.claim: Sign-off STA routinely reports timing violations that P&R never showed even when the design is unchanged, because the two environments model the same circuit differently.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Model mismatch between implementation and sign-off tools is a structural source of schedule risk; tools that close this gap carry value.
insights.quote: Nothing in the design changed between those two runs.
insights.locator: Every physical design engineer knows the moment

insights.claim: Chasing absolute WNS targets inside the P&R tool is the wrong approach; engineers should target relative improvements across P&R stages that translate predictably to sign-off.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Signals a methodology shift toward correlation-aware flows rather than local-tool metric optimization.
insights.quote: a WNS target hit in P&R means little when sign-off reads the same layout differently
insights.locator: The wrong response is to chase absolute markers

insights.claim: Comparison between P&R and sign-off must be done path by path (same startpoint, endpoint and corner), because aggregate WNS can hide paths moving in opposite directions.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Path-level correlation analytics are the useful diagnostic, not summary slack numbers.
insights.locator: Two runs can report different WNS

insights.claim: Plotting the convergence delta as a histogram is diagnostic: a tight distribution with a near-constant offset points to a global setting (derates, corner definition, library version), while a wide spread with a long tail points to extraction on specific nets or the clock network.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: A cheap triage heuristic that determines which fix is needed before iterating the design.
insights.quote: A wide spread with a long tail points at extraction on specific nets or at the clock network.
insights.locator: Plot the delta as a histogram

insights.claim: P&R tools use fast parasitic approximations repeated thousands of times during optimization, while sign-off extraction models the finished layout in full 3D (metal thickness, spacing, coupling capacitance, metal fill, via stacks), so the same net gets different R and C values.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Extraction accuracy/runtime trade-off is a fundamental source of correlation gaps, worsening at advanced nodes.
insights.locator: Puzzle 1: the post-route to sign-off bridge

insights.claim: The recommended method is to tune the implementation extractor against sign-off on a sample of long routes until they agree within a small margin, then freeze both sides and stop chasing exact mimicry, which is computationally out of reach.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Exact tool-to-tool correlation is infeasible; practical flows rely on calibrated offsets and directional trends.
insights.quote: Past that point, stop chasing exact mimicry. It is computationally out of reach

insights.claim: Delay-calculation differences between engines (slew interpolation, input pin capacitance handling, crosstalk delta delay) may add only a few picoseconds per stage but become a budget item across deep paths; sign-off also checks more scenarios, sometimes with newer libraries or unmodeled voltage/temperature points.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Scenario coverage mismatch between implementation and sign-off is a hidden schedule risk.
insights.quote: Per stage, the difference could be a few picoseconds. Across a deep stage path, it is a budget item.

insights.claim: On-chip variation (OCV) derating mismatches between implementation and sign-off shift every path at once, growing with path length, and clock-network derates applied in only one environment move setup and hold in opposite directions.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Setup-file consistency is a low-cost, high-impact control point for timing closure.
insights.quote: On-chip variation derating is the easiest source to get wrong.
insights.locator: On-chip variation derating is the easiest

insights.claim: Placement engines rewarded on virtual-wire timing tend to pack critical-path cells tightly, creating congestion that forces detailed-routing detours whose real wire R and C far exceed placement estimates.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Pre-route timing gains bought with density are illusory; flows need routability-aware placement.
insights.quote: The placer set a physical trap, and the router pays for it.

insights.claim: Pre-route congestion maps and the growth of the negative-slack (TNS) endpoint population are early indicators of post-route timing reality.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Early predictive signals let teams avoid costly late-stage rework.
insights.locator: Resolving this puzzle is a reading habit

insights.claim: Distributed cell utilization bounds and localized padding around choke points cost a little area and pre-route slack but recover far more slack after routing; a pre-route gain bought with density usually arrives at sign-off as a loss.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Trading small area for predictability is net-positive for closure and schedule.
insights.quote: a pre-route gain bought with density usually arrives at sign-off as a loss

insights.claim: Pre-CTS timing assumes ideal clocks with zero skew and delay, so data paths that close at placement can fail setup or hold after clock tree synthesis inserts real buffers, insertion delay and skew driven by OCV, voltage drop and metal-layer changes.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: The CTS transition is a predictable failure point that realistic clock modeling can de-risk.
insights.locator: Puzzle 3: the pre-clock to post-clock shift

insights.claim: Configuring pre-CTS environments with realistic, data-driven clock latency and skew models matching the target clock topology lets paths arrive at CTS with margin so post-clock reports confirm pre-clock ones.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Topology-aware pre-CTS modeling is a lever for fewer post-CTS iterations.

insights.claim: The P&R-to-sign-off pipeline should be treated as one continuous correlation map across three transitions (pre-clock to post-clock, pre-route to post-route, post-route to sign-off), since decisions made under ideal conditions cascade through all three.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Supports demand for integrated, correlation-aware EDA flows spanning implementation and sign-off.
insights.quote: Decisions made under ideal conditions cascade through all three transitions.

insights.claim: Modeling sign-off checks early in the P&R flow keeps fixes cheap; deltas found after detailed routing become ECO work because placement is frozen and routing channels are full.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Shift-left of sign-off analysis reduces costly late ECO cycles and schedule risk.
insights.quote: A delta found after detailed routing gets a harder reception: placement is frozen, routing channels are full, and the fix becomes ECO work.
insights.locator: Model sign-off checks inside the implementation flow

insights.claim: Designs built from the start for robustness and predictability alongside PPA can absorb late-stage functional ECO cycles while holding PPA flat, per an engineer with fifteen years on high-frequency CPU and networking ASIC blocks.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Predictability as a first-class design goal limits PPA erosion from late changes.
insights.locator: Model sign-off checks inside the implementation flow
